name: Fir Green
lede: Fir Green is a dark, muted green whose name points to the fir tree, a descriptive name with no recorded inventor.

sections.title: The name
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines fir green, also spelled with a hyphen, as a dark muted green [1]. It appears in his index of green names among the greens, near bottle green, Brunswick green and forest-green [2]. Who first used it, and when, is undocumented in the books we hold.

The same dictionary lists fire-red and fire-orange on the neighboring lines, which are unrelated: fir and fire are only alphabet neighbors [1]. Nearby in our names are [[forest-green]], [[hunter-green]] and [[pine-green]].

sections.title: What the swatch shows
sections.body: The swatch is a very dark, slightly blue green, close to black on many phone screens. As with any tree name, one swatch cannot hold a tree that changes with season and light.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch matches 451 of 23,781 archive paintings (1.9%, as photographed), more common than 75% of the named colors [3]. It peaks in the 1900s, in 3.5% of 1,674 paintings, 2.7 times the rate expected from the same museums [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a shadow, in 40% of the 272 paintings that hold it [3]. The most devoted painter is Harald Giersing, in 6 of 23 works here [3]. These are photographs of varnished paintings, so dark greens may be darkened by age.
